SK5010 A pattern that can backtrack, with nothing bounding how long it may take

A nested unbounded quantifier makes a near-match take exponential time, and no timeout means nothing stops it.

CategorySecurity
Default severitywarning
ScopeSemantic
Needs a compilationyes
Runs under --load=looseno
Cached per fileyes
Fixno
Language version floor—
Since2.0

Why

A backtracking engine, asked to match ^(a+)+$ against thirty as and a b, has to try every way of splitting those thirty characters between the inner + and the outer one before it can report failure — and there are 2^29 of them. That is the whole attack: no memory is allocated, no error is logged, nothing looks wrong on a dashboard, and one request holds a thread until the process is restarted. A handful of such requests is a denial of service against a machine that is otherwise idle, which is why this is a vulnerability rather than a performance note. Two things fix it and both are one argument in the same expression as the pattern. A matchTimeout bounds the damage without changing which inputs match: the engine throws RegexMatchTimeoutException when it has spent too long, and the caller decides what a too-slow input means. RegexOptions.NonBacktracking removes the cause instead of bounding it — it selects an automaton-based engine whose running time is linear in the input no matter what the pattern looks like — at the price of refusing lookarounds, backreferences and atomic groups at construction time, so it is the better answer where the pattern does not use them. ⚠ There is no fix on the diagnostic because neither answer can be chosen mechanically: a timeout value is a policy decision about how long this particular call is allowed to take, and NonBacktracking throws at run time on a pattern that uses a construct it does not support, so an edit that compiled would not be an edit that worked.

Example

Instead of:

if (Regex.IsMatch(input, @"^(\w+)+$")) {
    Accept(input);
}

Write:

if (Regex.IsMatch(input, @"^(\w+)+$", RegexOptions.None, TimeSpan.FromMilliseconds(100))) {
    Accept(input);
}

When it does not fire

⚠ The rule is deliberately much narrower than its own title, and the reference trees are why. Sonar's S6444 reports every regex constructed or matched without a timeout; on this repository's two reference trees that is sixteen findings and not one of them is a vulnerability — twelve are Assert.Matches(new Regex(@"MaxLevels\s*=\s*4")) in Vixen's own tests, matching a fixed pattern against source the tool itself had just produced. A security rule that reports a test assertion is how a reviewer learns to skim past every security finding the tool makes, so this rule reports only a pattern it can read and prove dangerous, and says nothing about the rest. Three conditions must all hold. The pattern must be a compile-time constant, because whether an unknown pattern backtracks is a question about another method — Newtonsoft.Json's Regex.IsMatch(input, patternText, GetRegexOptions(optionsText)) is silence for that reason, and so is a RegexOptions argument that is not constant, because whether it carries NonBacktracking is a question about the mitigation. ⚠ The outer quantifier must be unbounded, and Serilog is why: (\.(?<argument>[A-Za-z0-9]*)){0,1} in KeyValuePairSettings is a quantified group whose body carries a quantifier, which is the shape a naive detector matches, and it cannot blow up because {0,1} admits one iteration. ⚠ And the group's body must be exactly one quantified atom — (a+)+, ([a-z]*)*, ((ab)+)+ — which is narrower than "the body contains a quantifier" on purpose: (abc*)+ matches the wider test and is safe, because every iteration must begin with ab and there is almost nothing to backtrack through. The cost of the strictness is coverage, stated rather than hidden: ^(\w+\s?)*$ is a real ReDoS with two atoms in the body and this rule is silent on it, and an atomic group (?>…) and every lookaround are skipped rather than guessed at. ⚠ It ships at warning where the rest of this range ships at error, and the reason is not that it fires more. The other four are wrong unconditionally — a certificate callback that returns true, a DES key, a resolved DTD. This one is a vulnerability only if something an attacker influences reaches it, and the rule does not establish that; a catastrophic pattern matched against a constant is a latent hazard rather than a hole, and failing a build over it would be asserting a fact the rule did not check.
